name: Let it Burn

ways.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A splits left. Cross Mountaineer Creek a second time on a log bridge, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to three hours depending on load.

Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water; the basin and the wall are dry, though a spring at the base of the boulder field below the formation has been reported and should not be relied on.

The shorter of the two ways into the west basin: from the lake's north end, cross the outlet below the small dam and follow a climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the wall — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the actual base.

ways.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
ways.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
ways.notes:
The longer southern option, which avoids the outlet crossing. From Colchuck Lake follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, gaining talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds wet snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history.

Cut north / climber's-left off the Aasgard trail through a band of dense slide alder and heather — genuinely a bushwhack, 15 to 20 minutes, with a cairned path through it if you can find it. Once past the alder, take the left-most gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the west basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake.

priorPrimaryResearch: The outlet climbers' path (v0) is the shorter, recommended way into the west cirque below Colchuck Balanced Rock; the paragraph actually describes the Aasgard-trail / brush / gully line (v1) despite mentioning the outlet.

name: Beckey Route (Southwest Face)

ways.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
ways.season: Jul-Sep (dry)
ways.notes:
Park at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of SR-20, roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required and the lot is small enough that it fills on summer weekends.

Walk the maintained Blue Lake Trail for about 1.7 miles. The turnoff is a signed junction — the sign points straight on for Blue Lake and left for Liberty Bell Trail #727, Climbing Access — and it sits just past a small stream in a meadow, with a large cairn beside it. That stream is the last water you can count on.

Trail #727 climbs hard through granite slabs, talus and heather benches toward the gully that drains the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. In the gully itself the loose ground is least bad if you keep to climber's left for the lower two thirds, then cross and hug climber's right for the rest. Where the boot path forks a couple of hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch; the right branch leads on toward Lexington and Concord's south side.

ways.name: Early-season snow gully to the notch
ways.season: Highway opening (typically mid-late Apr or early May) through late Jun
ways.notes:
The same line as the summer approach, but the upper gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch commonly holds snow into late June and the boot path through the slabs and heather may be buried lower down. Parties carry an ice axe, and crampons if the snow has refrozen overnight.

SR-20 over Washington and Rainy Passes is gated every winter — it typically closes in late November or early December and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early May, with the exact dates set by snowpack and avalanche conditions rather than a calendar. Until the gate opens there is no drive-up access to the Blue Lake Trailhead at all.

priorPrimaryResearch: Summer Blue Lake Trail approach is the standard; variant 1 is the same line with early-season snow.

name: Liberty Cap via Ptarmigan Ridge

ways.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan crest
ways.season: June to early July
ways.notes: The prettier of the two ways in, and the one that puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom. Mowich Lake sits at about 4,929 ft at the end of a road that has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed in April 2025 (before that it was often snowed shut into early or mid July), and that single fact decides whether this approach is available at all. From the lake it is three to four miles of trail up through Spray Park; at about 6,400 ft a beaten path breaks off right toward the permanent snow. Cross the Flett Glacier in the gap between Echo Rock, 7,870 ft, and Observation Rock, 8,364 ft, at somewhere around 7,500 ft, climb to the saddle immediately east of Observation Rock, and cross onto the Russell Glacier near 7,800 ft. From there the crest runs south, sometimes on rock but mostly on easy snow just left of the crest line, with the Russell falling away east. This stretch is uncrevassed and is genuinely a walk. The last few hundred yards to camp are not: the crest narrows to a knife edge with an overhanging rock step on it, and most parties bypass that by dropping about 200 ft onto 40 degree snow on the east side and traversing back. Well above the base, the exit gully through the rock buttress is the one identification climbers argue about — whether it is the first or the second break in the cliffs is genuinely unsettled, so climb to the fixed pin rather than to a count. The descent is the Emmons route out to White River, so coming in this way needs a car shuttle or a very long road walk.

ways.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon
ways.season: Mid-May to early July
ways.notes: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.

priorPrimaryResearch: Mowich Lake/Spray Park is the usual summer approach to Ptarmigan Ridge (v0 puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom); White River/St Elmo (v1) is the early-season option before Mowich road opens. Paragraph describes both. Seasons already differ.

name: Liberty Crack

ways.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
ways.season: Jul-Sep (dry talus)
ways.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is not approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the west side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Some parties instead rappel the East Face to return directly to their packs.

ways.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
ways.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
ways.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.

priorPrimaryResearch: Both variants use the same SR-20 hairpin approach. Variant 1 is early-season snow conditions on it. The paragraph describes variant 0.

name: West Face - West Rib (Lichtenhorn / West Peak)

ways.name: Smith Brook road trailhead via Union Gap
ways.notes: From the trailhead on Smith Brook road, climb to Union Gap on the crest trail and follow it toward Lake Valhalla and Lichtenberg Pass, then leave the trail for the base of the west face.

ways.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass
ways.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and follow the crest trail north to Lake Valhalla, arriving from the west below the face. It is a few miles longer than the Smith Brook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.

name: North Slopes

ways.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
ways.season: late Jul-early Oct
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's left of the cliff bands. Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
ways.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
ways.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.

priorPrimaryResearch: Both variants are the same Aasgard line split by season; snow-free late Jul-early Oct is the normal season. Prose describes the line with snow caveats; closest to variant 0.

name: Northeast Face

ways.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
ways.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
ways.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.

ways.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
ways.season: July to September.
ways.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.

ways.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
ways.season: July to September.
ways.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.

ways.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
ways.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
ways.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph and v0 describe the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail to Dutch Miller Gap as standard; Necklace Valley and Pete Lake are longer alternatives.

ways.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
ways.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
ways.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.

ways.name: White River Campground and the Wonderland Trail to Summerland
ways.notes: The Fryingpan Creek trailhead and its spur trail are closed for the bridge replacement, planned to last into 2029. Park at White River Campground, where parking is limited, and follow the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. From Summerland the climb is unchanged: the climbers' path to Meany Crest, the Fryingpan Glacier and Whitman Notch.

ways.name: From Paradise across the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers
ways.season: Nov-May, while the White River road to Summerland is shut
ways.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.

name: South Route

ways.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
ways.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
ways.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.

ways.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (road closed at milepost 4)
ways.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
ways.notes: Not usable while the Suiattle River Road stays closed at milepost 4 under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner; washouts cut off the Downey Creek Trailhead, and the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) also closes the trailhead and the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails from August 15 through December 31, 2026. Before the closure this was the other end of the same corridor. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown, with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge; from there the route climbs to Spire Col, descends the Dana Glacier to White Rock Lakes, and regains the col on Lizard's south ridge from the lakes.

priorPrimaryResearch: For Lizard as the objective (South Route) the Downey/Bachelor Creek line is the shorter, 'accepted' approach per the route prose and variant 1's own notes; the Cascade Pass line is the Ptarmigan Traverse through-trip on which Lizard is a side trip.

name: West Ridge

ways.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
ways.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
ways.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.

ways.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
ways.season: Jul-Oct; the better late-season option
ways.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.

priorPrimaryResearch: Commonwealth Basin is the classic approach to Lundin, and the Cave Ridge traverse is a less-used alternative. The paragraph describes both as standard. The seasons already differ.

ways.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Three other approaches exist off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.

ways.name: From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail
ways.notes: Gentler, though not shorter. Drop north from Slate Pass to the Robinson Creek trail along the Middle Fork Pasayten, then near the big meadow horse camp take the Ferguson Lake trail, which descends about seven miles to Eureka Creek just south of the peak. From there, pick a line up the south side or into the basin between Monument and Lake Mountain.

name: Eel Glacier / Flypaper Pass

ways.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
ways.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
ways.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road about 8.5 miles to the road-end parking and leave the car there; the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood, and the washout itself is about a mile farther on. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.

ways.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west
ways.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
ways.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a trail the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.

priorPrimaryResearch: Dosewallips/West Fork to Anderson Pass is the standard Eel Glacier approach (Mountaineers route page, WTA 2024-25 reports); Enchanted Valley is the longer western alternative. Prose describes variant 0.
